1aynaad:366: The core problem of an AI Coding Agent memory system is not "what to remember", but "at what cost and at which layer it gets recalled". This reframes memory from a storage-capacity problem into a recall-path design problem. The four-layer mechanism has distinct latency and cost characteristics: hot memory (MEMORY.md/USER.md) is injected into the system prompt as a frozen snapshot at the start of each session, with zero latency but a persistent drain on the prompt token budget; session_search uses FTS5 full-text search through database queries, keeping costs controllable but relying on summary quality; skills are an index loaded on demand, expanded only when actually executed; external user models use asynchronous prefetch and do not block the current turn. This layering aligns exactly with the Agent Harness working-set idea: only the working set genuinely needed for the current turn goes into the window, and assets outside the window are wired in through explicit recall paths. Memory layering is a natural extension of context governance, not an isolated pile of capabilities.

1mj9t72:315: Skills are called procedural memory, and this name reveals their true design intent: they are not logs recording "what happened this time", but SOPs encoding "how to do this type of task next time". Factual memory answers "what is the environment", session retrieval answers "what happened before", and Skills answer "when encountering a type-X problem, what steps should be taken". If a team repeatedly runs into the same type of problem, encoding the solution as a skill rather than leaving it in chat history is real knowledge accumulation. Skills also introduce a unique risk: once a wrong experience is solidified, it is harder to correct than an ordinary mistake, because the skill will be triggered repeatedly in the future. So skills must have explicit lifecycle management: they must be creatable, updatable, deletable, annotatable with scope of applicability, and ideally accompanied by verification steps and failure modes.

1tqia55:292: Long-session compression is a challenge every long-running Agent faces. Compression itself is nothing new; the real difficulty is whether the Agent can still do useful work afterwards. If you don't proactively migrate key state to durable memory before compression, that state is permanently lost afterwards. The memory flush mechanism embeds state-migration logic before compression: before history is worn thin, the Agent gets a dedicated opportunity to write facts worth keeping long-term (user preferences, repeated corrections, stable conventions) to the hot-memory layer, and only then does compression execute. This is essentially taking a checkpoint before the history is worn thin. This principle can be generalized to any Agent system with compression: there must be an explicit state-migration opportunity before compression, otherwise "remembering" is empty talk in engineering terms.

zim2b1:335: Hot memory is a short card injected into the system prompt at the start of each session. Designing the boundaries of this layer matters more than directly adding a vector store. Hot memory must be small enough (MEMORY.md defaults to 2,200 characters, USER.md defaults to 1,375 characters) and should only hold high-value facts that must be known every turn: user preferences, stable environment conventions, repeated pitfalls and corrections. The character limit rather than token limit is a simple but correct engineering choice: it makes hot memory sizing completely independent of any particular model's tokenizer, so hot memory capacity remains effective when migrating across models. Write boundaries matter just as much. Hot memory encourages saving user preferences, environment facts, and stable conventions; it explicitly discourages saving current task progress, results of the current session, temporary TODOs, and one-off debugging paths. Once memory content enters the system prompt, it becomes part of the prompt supply chain and must be subject to input validation and permission management at that level.
